::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: The Generalized Price Equation: A Unified Framework for Selection by Consequences

text.text: I propose a formal theory of selection by consequences building on the generalized Price equation (GPE), which replaces the standard parent-offspring relation used in biological models of selection with a graded recurrence relation between two arbitrary sets.
The GPE thus provides an overarching framework for behavioral selection across all levels of analysis: evolution, culture, and learning.
I further adopt the GPE to derive a quantitative model of selection by consequences, alongside a simple method of statistical estimation, and sketch its empirical application using simulated data.
The proposed framework formally links evolutionary theory with operant learning and offers a new methodological approach to the analysis of behavioral data.
The idea that individual learning can be understood as a selection process is a recurrent theme in behavior analysis.
For example, Thorndike conjectured that learning "is a process of selection among reactions [...] within individuals" (Thorndike, 1900, p. 91).
text.formatted: For example, Thorndike conjectured that learning "is a process of selection among reactions [...] within individuals" <ref type="bibr">(Thorndike, 1900, p. 91)</ref>.

text.text: Since then, several authors have promoted the idea that individual behavior is shaped by processes that are analogous to evolution (e.g., Broadbent, 1961; Campbell, 1956; Gilbert, 1970; Herrnstein, 1961; Pringle, 1951; Staddon & Simmelhag, 1971). Skinner (1981) even proposed an overarching theoretical principle for evolution, culture and learning, which he called "selection by consequences."

For example, Donahoe et al. (1993) hold that selection of behavior requires an analogy between neurophysiology and genetics, whereas Baum (2017) approaches the problem in purely behavioral terms. text.text: Despite considerable advances in recent years, these different approaches to behavioral selection remain fragmented and lack an overarching perspective that unifies them at a theoretical level and goes beyond a shared vocabulary that is borrowed from evolutionary biology.
The aim of this article is to provide such a unifying theoretical framework.
In the following, I will present a formal model of selection by consequences based on a generalized version of the Price equation (Price, 1970; 1972).
text.formatted: In the following, I will present a formal model of selection by consequences based on a generalized version of the Price equation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Price, 1970;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">1972)</ref>.

text.text: To achieve this, I will first clarify what exactly is meant by the term "selection" and specify the class of systems (be it biological, behavioral, or physical) to which it applies.
I will then propose a quantitative theory that captures all processes of behavioral selection, irrespective of their physiological or computational foundations.

To demonstrate the feasibility of the framework, I will demonstrate how the proposed framework can be used to statistically estimate the amount of selection in behavioral experiments using simulated data.

Finally, I will discuss the implications and scope of the theory, including its relation to existing formal theories of behavioral selection, such as the Evolutionary Theory of Behavior Dynamics (McDowell, 2004), the Behavioral Price Equation (Baum, 2017), the Unified Reinforcement Principle (Donahoe et al., 1993), and the Multilevel Model of Behavioral Selection (Borgstede & Eggert, 2021).

Instead, I shall start with an accessible presentation of the PE and move straight to its generalization to so-called "fuzzy" systems (i.e., structures where sets and relations have no clear boundaries) as introduced in Borgstede (2025).

text.text: This generalized Price equation (GPE) will then be used to state the formal core of behavioral selection.
Formally, the PE is a simple mathematical identity.
In its standard form, it states that the change in average trait value 𝛥𝛥𝑧𝑧̅ can always be decomposed into a selection term, Cov(𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 , 𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 ), and a residual term, E(𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 ).

The selection term equals the covariance between individual trait values 𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 and the individual contribution to the future population ("fitness") 𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 , where 𝑖𝑖 ranges over the individuals of the present population.
The residual term takes the expected value over all deviations between parental trait values and the average trait values of their offspring Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 , each weighted by parental fitness 𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 .

text.text: Furthermore, the PE still holds if transmission from parents to offspring is mediated by nongenetic mechanisms.
For example, in mammals, food preferences are partially transmitted via the composition of mothers' milk (Jablonka & Lamb, 2005).

text.text: Transmission from parents to offspring may even be mediated by nonbiological factors, such as education or socialization processes.
In other words, children can acquire certain behavioral tendencies from their parents even if the behavior is not transmitted genetically.

Other example applications of the PE outside biology include social selection processes, such as college admission based on high-school grades, or even physical selection, such as evaporation (i.e., a decrease in mean particle motion) at a liquid surface (Borgstede, 2025).

text.text: 2   Despite its great generality, the standard PE only applies to systems where transmission is realized by a "crisp" parent-offspring relation.
In other words, an offspring either descends from a parent or not.
However, there are certain instances of selection where transmission is a matter of degree.
One prominent biological example can be found in social insects, such as honeybees or ants.

These species have a haplo-diploid set of chromosomes, which means that females have two sets of chromosomes (i.e., they are diploid), whereas males have only one set of chromosomes (i.e., they are haploid).
When a female lays an egg, it contains only one copy of the two chromosome sets, which may hatch without fertilization and thus yield a haploid offspring (i.e., a male).
If, however, an egg is fertilized, it receives a second set of chromosomes from the fertilizing male, yielding a diploid offspring (i.e., a female).

The genetic contribution from parents to offspring is thus no longer equal for all parents and all offspring, but depends on both, the parent's and the offspring's sex (resulting in sisters being genetically more strongly related with each other than with their mothers).
In terms of the PE, we might say that haplo-diploid species have graded degrees of parenthood.
The graded nature of parenthood becomes even more obvious in the context of nongenetically transmitted characteristics, such as social milieus or religious practices.
Such characteristics are not only inherited from biological parents, but also from genetically unrelated individuals, resulting in a process of cultural selection.

Cultural selection in this sense involves transmission of behavior from cultural "parents" (we might call them influencers) to cultural "offspring" (we might call them followers) -but the amount of transmission is not clear-cut.

text.text: Although present behavior is often influenced by past behavior (such as lever press rate in an operant conditioning experiment), there is no observable parent-offspring relation between "parent-behaviors" and "offspring-behaviors."
Moreover, it is questionable whether such a crisp mapping from past to present behavior actually exists.
As argued in Borgstede and Eggert (2021), such a mapping would require to specify exactly which of the "offspring-behaviors" descends from which "parent-behaviors."

text.text: Instead of a crisp parent-offspring relation, present behavior is most likely influenced by several past behaviors to various degrees.
Specifically, past behaviors with strong positive or negative consequences will have a larger influence on present behavior than past behaviors with less extreme consequences.

Therefore, a formal theory of behavioral selection requires to generalize the PE, such that it equally applies to crisp parent-offspring relations (such as literal parenthood between mother/father and their children) and graded levels of transmission from an arbitrary number of "parents" to an arbitrary number of "offspring" (such as differential transmission of responding depending on the amount of obtained food).

text.text: Fuzzy sets are sets where the membership of each object is expressed by a continuous function.
Similarly, fuzzy relations are relations where the degree of relatedness is expressed by a continuous function (Zadeh, 1965).

text.text: In a nutshell, the GPE generalized the concept of two crisp sets ("parents" and "offspring") that are related by a crisp mapping ("parenthood") to cases where the two sets may have unclear boundaries (such as past and present behaviors) and the relation may vary in degree (such as various degrees of influence from past to present behaviors).
In the following, I apply the GPE introduced in Borgstede (2025) to the domain of individual behavior, with some minor deviations with regard to the scaling of parameters.

text.text: Due to the greater scope of the GPE, it appears reasonable to depart from the traditional, biologically inspired, vocabulary.
Whereas in the standard PE, the index 𝑖𝑖 ranges over individuals, the GPE does not require the 𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 to range over different individuals.
Instead, the trait values 𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 are merely required to be measurements 𝑖𝑖 taken for trait 𝑧𝑧.
Thus, the index 𝑖𝑖 may designate any distinguishable grouping of measurements, including, but not limited to, actual individuals.
In behavioral selection, the index may be interpreted as ranging over different points in time within a single individual (cf.
Baum, 2027), over behavioral repertoires (cf. McDowell, 2004), or over recurring contexts (cf. Borgstede & Eggert, 2021).
text.formatted: Baum, 2027), over behavioral repertoires <ref type="bibr">(cf. McDowell, 2004)</ref>, or over recurring contexts (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Borgstede & Eggert, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Following this more general conceptual framework, the notions of "parents" and "offspring" are replaced by the more abstract concepts of sources and outcomes.
Accordingly, the mapping between the two distributions is no longer interpreted as "parenthood."
Instead, the GPE framework adopts the more abstract concept of recurrence, as suggested by Baum (2017).

text.text: This more abstract vocabulary avoids the metaphorical usage of concepts that have a clear interpretation in the context of natural selection, but are less clear when applied to behavioral selection (such as a "mother-behavior" and a "father-behavior" mating to produce "child-behaviors").
This change in wording does not imply that it is wrong to use the traditional, biologically inspired, vocabulary in the context of behavioral selection (such as in McDowell, 2004).

Given the conceptual and mathematical background of the GPE, it is now possible to provide a quantitative model of selection by consequences.
I will derive a minimal model that captures the core idea of behavior being selected by consequences within an individual, while being flexible enough to incorporate more complex mechanisms.
I will explain the model mainly informally, thereby limiting mathematical notation to the core equations.
A rigorous formalization, including all mathematical proofs, is provided in the Appendix.

The core idea of behavioral selection is that, as behavior varies within an individual, environmental contingencies (such as different schedules of reinforcement) produce a covariance between behavior and its consequences, which then acts as the main driver of subsequent behavior change (cf. Baum, 1973).
text.formatted: The core idea of behavioral selection is that, as behavior varies within an individual, environmental contingencies (such as different schedules of reinforcement) produce a covariance between behavior and its consequences, which then acts as the main driver of subsequent behavior change (cf. <ref type="bibr">Baum, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: However, not every covariance qualifies as an instance of selection.
Following the GPE, behavior must covary with fitness, which is defined as the average over all source recurrence weights.
Therefore, only consequences that are reliable proxies for fitness can be interpreted in terms of selection.
At the level of natural selection, such fitness proxies can easily be found, since biological fitness essentially relies on survival and reproduction.
Consequently, any event that is (directly or indirectly) predictive of survival or reproduction is a biological fitness predictor.

In previous work I have argued that statistical predictors of biological fitness (such as food) should also drive individual-level selection because individuals who adapt their behavior to increase such fitness predictors will, on average, have an evolutionary advantage over those who do not (Borgstede, 2020; Borgstede & Eggert, 2021).
text.formatted: In previous work I have argued that statistical predictors of biological fitness (such as food) should also drive individual-level selection because individuals who adapt their behavior to increase such fitness predictors will, on average, have an evolutionary advantage over those who do not <ref type="bibr">(Borgstede, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Borgstede & Eggert, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, Baum (2005) proposes that individual behavior is predominantly shaped by phylogenetically important events (PIE), which are events that are predictive of increases (or decreases) in biological fitness, such as signals for the availability of resources or mating opportunities but also signals of threat.

text.text: The idea that fitness predictors, rather than fitness itself, are the main driver of individual-level behavioral selection theoretically plausible but difficult to translate into a quantitative model, since the biological fitness of an individual is usually unknown (unless the individual is dead).

However, since the GPE can be directly applied to within-individual selection, it returns an explicit definition of behavioral fitness (i.e., average behavioral recurrence) and thus does not require a link to biological fitness to be empirically applicable.

Instead, one may specify behavioral fitness proxies with respect to behavioral recurrence directly, which leads itself to a straightforward implementation of behavioral fitness proxies into the GPE framework.
In a nutshell, if we can predict behavioral fitness from consequences, the empirical covariance between behavior and consequences is in fact sufficient for the calculation of behavioral selection.
The following basic model exploits such behavioral fitness predictors to derive an empirical approach to estimating the amount of selection by consequences within a single individual.
I start with the basic concepts of the GPE and their behavioral counterparts, followed by an implementation of the hypothesis that behavioral selection is essentially driven by consequences.
First and foremost, it needs to be clarified what the source and outcome measurements (𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 and 𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 ) are supposed to be, and how different realizations of these measurements vary over time.

The second step is the definition of fitness at a purely behavioral level (i.e., independent of biological fitness), such that empirical covariances between behavior and its consequences can be utilized to derive corresponding estimates of behavioral selection.
I will introduce these concepts informally here using a simple example, leaving the general case for the formal Appendix.
Imagine we are interested in how the behavior (e.g., lever pressing) of a certain individual is selected by consequences (e.g., food delivery).
The individual is repeatedly observed in subsequent sessions, each consisting of a certain number of trials (i.e., each session contains at least two behavioral measurements).
Suppose we make food delivery contingent on lever pressing and track the rates of responding and food delivery for every trial.
Now imagine we inspect the data of all trials in the first session -if food delivery is contingent on lever pressing, higher lever pressing rates necessarily come with higher rates of food delivery.
This contingency is an immediate consequence of the programmed schedule of reinforcement.

In other words, as long as the individual's behavior rate varies over trials, the realized contingency enforces a covariance between responses and consequences observed over several trials within a single session We can calculate the empirical covariance between response rate and food rate for every session, using the data observed in the respective trials.
In addition to this covariance, we may calculate the average response rate for each session, which we use to calculate the change in average behavior from one session to another.

Note that, in principle, the time scale does not matter -sessions may span over minutes, hours, or even days -as long as there are at least two observations in each session (two is a natural lower limit because a single observation has no variance and, consequently cannot covary with anything).
We can thus apply the same framework at different time scales, in line with the conceptual framework of multiscale behavior analysis (Baum, 2013; 2018).
text.formatted: We can thus apply the same framework at different time scales, in line with the conceptual framework of multiscale behavior analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baum, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">2018)</ref>.

text.text: Let us now introduce the GPE to our hypothetical scenario.

For any two adjacent sessions (called session one and session two hereafter), the response rates observed in session one are treated as the source measurements (𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 ) and the response rates observed in session two are treated as the outcome measurements (𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 ).
The change in mean trait value (Δ𝑧𝑧̅ ) is simply the difference in average response rate between any two adjacent sessions.
As required by the GPE, we center all measurements around the average response rate in session one.

Since the recurrence relation between source and outcome measurements is not given a priori (we cannot observe which past behavior influences which present behavior to which degree), we use the observed consequences (i.e., food rate) as a fitness proxy (𝑝𝑝 𝑖𝑖 ).

To quantify to which amount changes in food rate coincide with changes in behavioral fitness, we specify a linear regression of behavioral fitness on food rate (i.e., 𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 = 𝛽𝛽 0 + 𝛽𝛽 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 𝑝𝑝 𝑖𝑖 + 𝜀𝜀 𝑖𝑖 ).

text.text: The scaling factor (𝛽𝛽 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 ) equals the slope of the predictor's fitness function.
This slope tells us how much the expected value of behavioral fitness changes per unit change in obtained food rate.

If the fitness function is constant over all successive sessions, the free parameter 𝛽𝛽 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 can be estimated by means of a simple linear regression, where the average change in behavior in each session is predicted from the covariance between behavior and its consequences in each session.
If the fitness function changes over time, we may estimate 𝛽𝛽 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 as a function of the session index using a timevarying regression model, instead.

We further retrieve the expected values of the recurrence weights (𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ) for any two adjacent sessions by multiplying the values of the corresponding fitness predictors (i.e., obtained food rate) with the slope of the fitness function (i.e., 𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 = 𝛽𝛽 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 𝑝𝑝 𝑖𝑖 ).

We can thus construct an empirically derived recurrence matrix for every two adjacent sessions, which can then be used to partition the change in average behavior into a selection term and a non-selection term according to the GPE.
I will now illustrate the logic of the basic selection model using simulated data.
The example is intended to promote an intuitive understanding of the GPE and its application to behavior analysis.
Therefore, I keep the example as simple as possible and spare more sophisticated applications of the GPE for future work.
Imagine a single individual whose behavior is observed by consequences over subsequent sessions, each spanning over several trials.

For each trial we record the observed response rate and the obtained amount of food, such that the change in average response rate between sessions can be calculated for each pair of adjacent sessions.
We can further use the observed behavior and consequences to calculate the covariance between response rate and food rate for each session.

We will use these two quantities (average change and covariance between behavior and consequences) to estimate the slope of the fitness function, from which we can then derive the amount of behavioral selection between each pair of adjacent sessions.
To give a concrete numerical example, data was simulated for 20 successive sessions consisting of three trials each, using an iterative procedure.
First, the response rates (𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 ) for each trial in session one were randomly sampled from a normal distribution with mean 10 and standard deviation five.

The food rates (𝑝𝑝 𝑖𝑖 ) were generated for each trial using the feedback function of a variable ratio schedule (VI 1) of reinforcement with responses randomly distributed over time (cf. Nevin & Baum, 1980).
text.formatted: The food rates (𝑝𝑝 𝑖𝑖 ) were generated for each trial using the feedback function of a variable ratio schedule (VI 1) of reinforcement with responses randomly distributed over time <ref type="bibr">(cf. Nevin & Baum, 1980</ref>).

text.text: These food rates were then used to calculate the theoretical recurrence weights (𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ), such that the recurrence of each response rate is proportional to its consequences.
Formally, recurrence was generated using a linear model (𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 = 𝛽𝛽 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 𝑝𝑝 𝑖𝑖 + 𝜀𝜀 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ) with 𝛽𝛽 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 = 1 and an error standard deviation of 0.5.
These recurrence weights were used to calculate the expected response rates for session two according to the GPE (𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 = ∑ 𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 𝑖𝑖 𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 + Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 ).

The residuals of the resulting trial response rates in session two (Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 ) were realized by sampling from a normal distribution with expected value zero and standard deviation five (thereby implementing some random response variation).

The response rates of the trials in session two were then used to generate corresponding food rates as described above, which were further used to calculate new recurrence weights and so on till 20 sessions were complete.
To investigate the robustness of the proposed estimation procedure, the whole simulation was repeated 10,000 times.
To demonstrate how the selection model can be exploited empirically, I applied the CLOE to the data from all pairs of adjacent sessions.
First, the covariance between response rate and food rate (Cov(𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 , 𝑝𝑝 𝑖𝑖 )) was calculated for each session.
Second, the change in average response rate between every pair of adjacent sessions (Δ𝑧𝑧̅ ) was calculated.
These values were then fed into a linear regression of behavior change on covariance.
The simulation results confirm that the slope of this regression model is indeed identical to the parameter 𝛽𝛽 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 in the CLOE (M = 1, SD = 0.11, N = 10,000).
Given this parameter, behavioral selection can be estimated for each pair of adjacent sessions by means of Equation 2.

In this paper, I introduced a quantitative model of selection by consequences building on the generalized Price equation (GPE, Borgstede, 2025).
text.formatted: In this paper, I introduced a quantitative model of selection by consequences building on the generalized Price equation <ref type="bibr">(GPE, Borgstede, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The GPE provides an abstract description of how selection works, irrespective of the units of selection and the specific underlying mechanisms.
Most importantly, it replaces the concept of parenthood between parents and offspring with a graded recurrence relation that connects source measurements with outcome measurements.

I used the GPE to derive a formal model of selection by consequences, which yielded the covariance based law of effect (CLOE) as a fundamental principle, as well as a straightforward estimation procedure for the amount of behavioral selection using standard linear regression.
The proposed selection framework has wide implications for behavior analysis.
From a pragmatic view, the GPE can be understood as a comparatively simple tool for the statistical analysis of behavioral data.
However, the GPE is much more than a statistical model -it is the formalization of a fundamental theoretical principle: selection by consequences.
As such, it clarifies in which respect behavior change at the individual level (learning) mirrors behavior change at the population level (culture) and at the species level (evolution).
Moreover, the framework is scalable to include different levels of selection, simultaneously (see Borgstede et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Moreover, the framework is scalable to include different levels of selection, simultaneously (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Borgstede et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Being a mathematical identity, the GPE is more than an empirically derived law -it is a theoretical commitment to the idea that behavior is best analyzed in terms of selection (cf. Borgstede & Luque, 2021).
text.formatted: Being a mathematical identity, the GPE is more than an empirically derived law -it is a theoretical commitment to the idea that behavior is best analyzed in terms of selection (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Borgstede & Luque, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: What makes such fundamental principles useful is that they provide an abstract formal vocabulary for a certain theoretical approach and thus point researchers towards what to look for.

In other words, the GPE allows us to analyze any process of behavior change in terms of selection, thereby telling us that the essential part of behavior analysis lies in understanding the mechanisms underlying behavioral recurrence.

The present paper is only a first step towards developing a corresponding methodology for the empirical estimation and evaluation of GPE based selection models, which will be addressed in future work.
One important feature of the GPE is that it treats behavioral selection as a molar concept.
In other words, selection always acts at the level of average trait values (𝑧𝑧̅ ).
Consequently, the GPE makes no a-priori assumptions about the molecular mechanisms underlying selection.

At the evolutionary level, for example, recurrence may be largely mediated by the genetic architecture of a specieshowever, average behavior may also be partially transmitted by non-genetic factors such as parental instructions or a tendency of children to imitate their parents' behavior.
The same holds for the cultural level, where recurrence probably builds on several mechanisms such as imitation and instruction.
At the level of individual learning, selection is very likely mediated by various molecular mechanisms, which feed into the recurrence relation.

Whereas the basic selection model introduced in this paper focuses on the role of behavioral consequences, other pathways of behavioral recurrence are possible, including time-dependent or history-dependent recurrence weights.
In other words, the recurrence weights in the GPE can be an arbitrary function of past behavior, context effects, or learning history, resulting in context-dependent predictors of behavioral fitness.

Interestingly, although the concept of behavioral selection is intrinsically linked to the molar paradigm of behavior analysis, its application to model building still requires informed hypotheses about the molecular mechanisms underlying behavioral recurrence.
In other words, although the level of analysis is molar, the GPE acknowledges the importance of studying molecular mechanisms.

One might say that selection by consequences provides a molar account of average behavior change (in terms of selection), in the same way as thermodynamics provides a molar account of average particle motion (in terms of heat).

In the following, I will briefly relate the GPE to existing formal approaches to behavioral selection, namely the Unified Reinforcement Principle (URP) by Donahoe (1993), the Evolutionary Theory of Behavior Dynamics (ETBD) by McDowell (2004 McDowell ( , 2013)), the Behavioral Price Equation (BPE) by Baum (2017), and the Multilevel Model of Behavioral Selection (MLBS) by Borgstede and Eggert (2021).

text.text: I will use the GPE as an analytic framework to compare these approaches.
Since the GPE is essentially a formal definition of selection, it tells us exactly which aspects of the different approaches are universal, and which are specific to the model.
Formally, every model that relates past observations to present observations can be locally approximated by a linear projection using a corresponding recurrence relation.
Consequently, at a very abstract level, all existing models of selection by consequences are special instances of the GPE.

However, they differ substantially regarding the units of selection (i.e., the range of the index 𝑖𝑖), the kinds of traits (i.e., the quality of the character 𝑧𝑧), and the mechanisms underlying behavioral recurrence (i.e., the values of 𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ). Donahoe et al. (1993) provide a formal model of behavior dynamics that is inspired by neural processes.

text.text: Their Unified Reinforcement Principle (URP) is formally implemented by artificial neural networks that evolve over time, which they call "selection networks."
The units of selection (𝑖𝑖) are collections of neurons, whereas the trait of interest (𝑧𝑧) is the firing rate of these neurons.

Consequently, if we were to apply the GPE to partition average behavior change into a selection and a residual component, we would have to calculate the average neural firing rate at one point in time and compare it to the average neural firing rate at a later point in time.

In other words, in the URP, selection occurs at the level of average firing rate varying over different neurons within trials, but not over different trials. Donahoe et al. (1993) make very specific assumptions about the molecular mechanisms of behavioral recurrence (𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ), which in their model corresponds to the dynamic equations of the neural network.
text.formatted: In other words, in the URP, selection occurs at the level of average firing rate varying over different neurons within trials, but not over different trials. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Donahoe et al. (1993)</ref> make very specific assumptions about the molecular mechanisms of behavioral recurrence (𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ), which in their model corresponds to the dynamic equations of the neural network.

text.text: In particular, they attempt to emulate parts of the neural system underlying behavior, rather than merely simulate behavioral dynamics.

However, the connection between their model and the theory of behavioral selection remains largely rhetorical (i.e., they make use of selectionist vocabulary), without making the analogy between operant learning and evolution explicit at a formal level.
McDowell (2004, 2013) follows a radically different path in his Evolutionary Theory of Behavior Dynamics (ETBD).
text.formatted: McDowell <ref type="bibr">(2004,</ref> <ref type="bibr">2013)</ref> follows a radically different path in his Evolutionary Theory of Behavior Dynamics (ETBD).

text.text: Instead of neural mechanisms, the ETBD focuses on the computations underlying behavioral dynamics, which is hypothesized to be equivalent to the computations implemented by natural selection.
The general approach of ETBD is to simulate (rather than emulate) behavior dynamics.
The units of selection (𝑖𝑖) are collections of potential behaviors that vary in a quantitative character (𝑧𝑧).
Like in the URP, the different values of 𝑧𝑧 are realized over different units (here: potential behaviors) at a particular point in time.
Formally, McDowell implements an evolutionary algorithm that is modeled after genetical selection occurring in sexually reproducing species.
Consequently, the ETBD introduces such concepts as "father-behaviors" and "mother-behaviors" who produce "child-behaviors."
The ETBD makes very specific assumptions about the computations of present behaviors from past behaviors.

Although, due to the complexity of the algorithm, it is difficult to derive precise functional relations between source and outcome measurements analytically, it would be possible to derive an approximate recurrence relation with specific values for the different recurrence weights (𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ).
Yet another proposal of formalizing behavioral selection was made by Baum (2017).
text.formatted: Yet another proposal of formalizing behavioral selection was made by <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baum (2017)</ref>.

text.text: His Behavioral Price Equation (BPE) is conceptually very similar to the account put forward in this article.
The units of selection (𝑖𝑖) are observed behaviors that vary over time in their intensity (𝑧𝑧), such as response frequency or time allocation.
However, since the BPE builds on the standard Price equation, Baum (2017) had to introduce some additional assumptions to make his model work.
text.formatted: However, since the BPE builds on the standard Price equation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baum (2017)</ref> had to introduce some additional assumptions to make his model work.

text.text: Specifically, the BPE defines fitness as the ratio of target behaviors during test sessions and training sessions (i.e., fitness is just the rate of increase in behavioral frequency).
Moreover, lacking an observable criterion for "parenthood" between behaviors, the BPE defines the recurrence weights (𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ) by means of numeric identity.
In other words, if an individual responds 20 times in a trial during session one, all trials in sessions two with 20 responses are treated as its "offspring."

Therefore, although the BPE is very general in that it does not rely on any specific molecular mechanisms, it is also quite limited in scope, since the way it implements the recurrence relation forces the residual part of the Price equation to be zero (cf. Borgstede & Eggert, 2021).

text.text: The purpose of this article was to adopt the generalized Price equation (GPE) for the level of individual behavior change and derive a quantitative model of selection by consequences that can be readily applied to behavioral data.

The proposed model builds on previous applications of the Price equation to behavioral selection but for the first time allows for the construction of empirically derived estimates of behavioral fitness.

The introduction of the GPE into behavior analysis is a major theoretical contribution, since it solves the long-standing problem of how the biological concepts of reproduction and inheritance can be linked to behavioral dynamics within individuals.
The more general concept of graded recurrence covers all levels of selection by consequences: evolution, culture, and learning.
The GPE also offers a consistent and scalable toolkit for the experimental analysis of behavior in terms of selection.

Therefore, in this article, I prefer to speak of "source measurements being related to outcome measurements," rather than "parents producing offspring."
Formally, the GPE divides measurements into 𝑛𝑛 source measurements 𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 and 𝑘𝑘 outcome measurements 𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 .
Consequently, Δ𝑧𝑧̅ is the mean difference between source and outcome measurements (in fact, even arbitrarily weighted means are admissible).
Contrary to the standard PE, transmission from sources to outcomes is a matter of degree.

Formally, the different degrees of relatedness are modeled by assigning a quantitative transmission weight 𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 ("gamma") to each pair of source and outcome measurements, resulting in a linear predictive model for each outcome measurement based on the totality of source measurements (i.e., 𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 = 1 𝑛𝑛 ∑ 𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 𝑖𝑖 𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 + Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 ).
In other words, each outcome measurement is described as a linear combination (i.e., a weighted sum) of the source measurements plus a residual term Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 .
The transmission weights form a fuzzy recurrence relation, which is entirely determined by a matrix containing all 𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 .

Individual fitness 𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 is defined for each source measurement 𝑖𝑖 as the average of all transmission weights originating from measurement 𝑖𝑖, taken over all outcome measurements 𝑗𝑗 (i.e., 𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 = 1 𝑘𝑘 ∑ 𝛾𝛾 𝑖𝑖𝑗𝑗 𝑗𝑗 ).
Finally, all outcome measurements are centered around the arithmetic mean of the source measurements.

Given these definitions, the change in mean trait value between the distribution of source measurements and outcome measurements can be partitioned into a covariance term (corresponding to the amount of change due to selection) and a residual term (capturing all other sources of change apart from selection), resulting in the generalized Price equation (GPE): 4 Δ𝑧𝑧̅ = Cov(𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 , 𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 ) + E(Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 � (2) Equation 2 closely resembles the standard PE.
However, due to the centering of source and outcome measurements, there is no need for weighting by average fitness.

Furthermore, whereas in the standard PE, the residual term is expressed by fitness-weighted deviations from parental trait values (𝑤𝑤 𝑖𝑖 Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑖𝑖 ), the GPE defines the residuals from the perspective of outcome measurements (Δ𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 ), thereby avoiding the fitness weighting.

In other words, residuals are defined as the difference between the observed outcome measurements 𝑧𝑧 𝑗𝑗 and the expected outcome measurements one would predict if there were no other sources of change apart from selection.
